Chapter 7: Embracing Self-Acceptance and Letting Go of Shame.
You know, there’s a turning point that sneaks up on you—so quietly, you might almost miss it. After years of trying to prove yourself, chasing approval, and working so hard to cover up the marks of poverty or difference, something shifts. Suddenly, you start seeing yourself with fresh eyes. That old, heavy shame that used to color every interaction? It starts to fade. And in its place, you find a gentle sense of acceptance.
It doesn’t happen all at once. It’s in those small, everyday moments. Maybe a student thanks you for believing in her. Maybe a friend shares a secret, trusting you with their softest side. Or you just catch yourself laughing more easily, speaking from the heart, not weighing every single word. It’s like those old fears—being found out, not being enough—well, they begin to lose their grip on you.
He remembers those early days, fresh in America, feeling hungry to belong and desperate to hide his past. But now, he can see it differently. All those struggles? They’re woven into his strength. The hard times, the missteps, the doubt—sure, they left their mark, but they don’t get to define who he is. Most people don’t realize just how much energy it takes to carry shame around—or how freeing it feels to finally set it down.
Of course, there are still tough days. Sometimes the old insecurities make a comeback. But they don’t run the show anymore. He’s learning to be kind to himself, to accept that growth isn't always a straight line, and that healing is something you work at, day by day. When he embraces his own story—messy, complicated, unfinished—it brings him a deep sense of peace.
And now, he shares this lesson with his students. He encourages them to accept their own stories, to find strength in their struggles. The classroom turns into a space for honesty, a place where making mistakes isn’t failure—it’s just part of learning. It becomes so clear: self-acceptance isn’t about being perfect. It’s about showing compassion—to yourself, and to everyone around you.
